items.prompt: White to move. White's c-pawn and Black's e-pawn have been exchanged off, so on the a-, b- and c-files White has two pawns (a2, b2) against three (a7, b7, c6). Which pawn move starts the minority attack?

b2 holds the white pawn.
a7 holds the black pawn.
b7 holds the black pawn.
c6 holds the black pawn.
No file is open; the c-file is half-open for White and the e-file for Black.
After b4 the pawn on b4 is attacked once by Black (the bishop on e7).
After b4 the pawn on b4 is defended once by White (the rook on b1).
At depth 16 b4, h3, Rfe1, Rbe1 and a3 are all within 0.4 pawn of the engine's best move.

hints: Count each side's pawns on the a-, b- and c-files. Which side has fewer?

items.explain: b4 begins the minority attack: two white pawns against three on the a- to c-files. After b4 the pawn is attacked once, by the bishop on e7, and defended once, by the rook on b1. At depth 16 b4 is one of several close moves (h3, Rfe1, Rbe1 and a3 are also within 0.4 pawn), so b4 is a sound way to start the plan here, not the only good move.

claims.statement: g3 holds the white bishop.

At depth 16 Nh5 is the engine's first choice.
At depth 16 Ne4 is rated at least two pawns worse than Nh5.

items.explain: Both Nh5 and Ne4 attack the bishop, so the idea alone does not choose the move. At depth 16 the engine rates Nh5 first and Ne4 at least two pawns lower. The cramped side often looks for exchanges (a rule of thumb); the specific move still has to be checked.

feedback_by_move.f6e4: Ne4 also attacks the bishop, but the engine rates it at least two pawns worse than Nh5 (depth 16). An exchange offer is not safe just because it is an exchange offer.
